## Question

<div class="chapter-question">When a model predicts an unobserved answer or study result, what exactly has been recovered?</div>

## Why this week belongs here

Week 7 introduces synthetic respondents and distributional validation. Week 8 will separate individual prediction, aggregate prediction, group differences and experimental-result forecasting rather than treating them as one achievement.

## Provisional core readings

- **Methods:** Kim and Lee (2026), “AI-Augmented Surveys.” Read the complete paper. It predicts unasked items for observed respondents using their other answers. [Preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.09620). [@KimLee2026]
- **Methods and validation:** Xie et al. (2026), “Evaluating the Statistical Realism of LLM-Generated Social Science Data.” Read the complete article. It tests whether synthetic data preserve more than a selected statistic. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2538145123). [@XieEtAl2026]
- **Substantive application:** Lax and Phillips (2009), “Gay Rights in the States,” *American Political Science Review*. Read the complete article. It uses multilevel regression and poststratification to estimate state opinion and study policy responsiveness on gay rights. It gives us an established comparison for claims about recovering quantities not observed directly. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0003055409990050). [@LaxPhillips2009]

Additional comparisons: Ashokkumar et al. (2026) on forecasting experimental results and Wang, Morgenstern and Dickerson (2025) on flattening within-group variation. [@AshokkumarEtAl2026; @WangMorgensternDickerson2025]

## Planned chapter and class arc

Begin with established approaches to missing data and prediction; distinguish the four inferential targets; compare the designs and validation evidence in the core papers; then build a matched-record example in which aggregate error is small despite large individual errors.

[See the provisional Week 8 Python plan](../python/session08.qmd).
